rows.supports: Alpha particles are two protons and two neutrons; gamma rays are photons, weightless packets of energy.
An alpha particle removes two protons and two neutrons from the parent nucleus.
Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass; gases such as air are matter.
Atoms are about 10^-10 m across; the nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller.

The becquerel is one disintegration per second; the gray is one joule of energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue; the sievert takes into account both the energy and the biological effects of the type of radiation, and measures tissue damage.
The becquerel measures activity, the gray measures absorbed dose and the sievert measures the biological effect of radiation.
A daughter nuclide may be stable or may decay itself; uranium-238 reaches stable lead-206 in 14 steps.
The uranium-238 and thorium-232 decay chains (optional card).

A Geiger counter detects the ionization of the gas in its tube; a scintillation counter uses a material that emits light when ionizing radiation excites it; dosimeters measure ionizing radiation and are often used to determine personal radiation exposure (the page's picture shows one worn on the chest).
Radiation is present all around us; background radiation comes mostly from natural minerals in the ground, soil and water, and from cosmic radiation.
Humans are exposed to natural radiation sources every day, and the level varies from place to place.

The threshold for acute radiation syndrome is about 1 sievert; effects are more severe at higher doses and dose rates; a low dose or one spread over a long time carries less risk because repair is more likely.

A very high exposure over a short time can cause nausea and vomiting within hours; low levels can add a small increase in the risk of cancer over a lifetime; about 99 percent of people given 100 millisieverts would not get cancer as a result.
The number of protons (the atomic number) defines the element.
IUPAC publishes the periodic table of the elements (optional card).
Half-life is the time for half of the radioactive atoms to decay; it ranges from seconds to billions of years.
Half-life and the exponential decay curve.
Each radioactive nuclide has a characteristic, constant half-life.

Ionizing radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms; non-ionizing radiation does not. Radio waves, visible light and microwaves are non-ionizing; alpha, beta, gamma and X-rays are ionizing.

Ionizing radiation is energetic enough to knock electrons out of molecules: high-energy ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays and particles such as alpha and beta. Lower-frequency, lower-energy electromagnetic radiation is nonionizing.
Ionizing radiation is radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, a process called ionization.
Radiation does not get on or in people; radioactive contamination can be spread. A contaminated person is exposed until the radioactive material is removed.

External irradiation stops when the source is shielded or the person moves outside the radiation field; material on skin or clothes can often be washed off; internal exposure stops when the radionuclide leaves the body.
Isotope definition and mass number.
Some forms of an element are stable and others unstable.
The three particles and their charges; the nucleus holds the majority of the atom’s mass.
The nucleus is an extremely small space at the center of an atom.
The gold-foil experiment (optional story).
Ionizing radiation can damage the DNA in cells; cells are extremely efficient at repairing it; damage not repaired correctly can kill a cell or eventually make it cancerous.
A person who was exposed to radiation is not radioactive.
Natural background radiation: radon, cosmic radiation and radioactive minerals in the ground and the body.
Becquerel found in 1896 that a uranium-rich rock darkens a photographic plate.
Potassium-40 in the human body.
Uranium and thorium decay chains in nature (optional card).
The average yearly dose is about 6.2 millisieverts and a whole body CT is about 10 millisieverts.
Acute radiation syndrome starts at about 1 sievert (1000 millisieverts); a low dose, or one spread over time, carries less risk.
Low levels do not cause immediate health effects but can add a small increase in the risk of cancer over a lifetime.
Isotopes of carbon, hydrogen and other elements, stable or with a half-life.
Stable and unstable forms of an element; unstable forms are radioactive.
Natural potassium-40 in the human body.
The average yearly dose is about 6.2 millisieverts, most of it from natural background radiation; a whole body CT is about 10 millisieverts.
The dose threshold for acute radiation syndrome is about 1 sievert (1000 millisieverts).

Limiting time, increasing distance and shielding all reduce a dose; barriers of lead, concrete or water protect from gamma rays; dentists place a lead apron on patients; more walls give more protection.
Alpha particles cannot penetrate the outer layer of skin; beta particles are stopped by a thin layer of aluminum; several inches of lead or a few feet of concrete may be required to stop gamma rays.
A sheet or two of paper, or the top layer of skin cells, usually stops alpha particles; beta particles are stopped by a thin layer of metal; gamma radiation is very penetrating.
Barriers of lead, concrete or water protect from gamma rays and X-rays; dentists place a lead apron on patients having X-rays of their teeth.
Radioactive decay is the spontaneous change of an unstable parent nuclide into a daughter nuclide.
A radionuclide is a radioactive (unstable) form of an element.
The radiation does not change with chemical state, temperature or pressure.
Decay is random for a single atom; it is impossible to predict when one will decay.
